summary:
Caraga is an administrative region of the Philippines with no region-specific statute, ordinance or regulation bearing on trans people recorded in the source material. A visitor there stands under national Philippine law, under which same-sex conduct is legal nationwide and no provision of law criminalises a person for being transgender; same-sex relations have never been criminalised. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, "Generally Safe", for LGBTQ+ travellers overall and 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the "Exercise Caution" band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81.

Caraga is, however, comparatively well covered by local anti-discrimination instruments. Butuan City, the regional capital, enacted a non-discrimination ordinance in 2016, and two of the eight Philippine provinces with SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances, Agusan del Norte and Dinagat Islands, lie within Caraga. Ordinances of this kind exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial level across the country, but they are the only protection on offer: no national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years since 2000 without passage.

Identity documents cannot be brought into line with a trans visitor's presentation. There is no administrative legal gender recognition. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A court order is the only route, so the marker carried at hotels, checkpoints and counters remains the one assigned at birth. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, which allies planned to endorse to the 20th Congress on 28 July.

The protections that do exist form a patchwork. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment. The Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

Executive-branch machinery exists on paper. Executive Order 100, series of 2019, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51, series of 2023, amended it to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee. Neither had been implemented as of 2025, so a visitor cannot rely on any federal diversity office for assistance.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days of each other: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos on the same day. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; she called the attack traumatic, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. The LGBT rights organisation Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIE Equality Bill, and the Commission on Human Rights described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex pairings are used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. There is no gender-matched placement. Official practice instead takes the form of administrative segregation: the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.

Social attitudes vary and are not protective. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, which bears directly on restroom use in Caraga's malls, transport terminals and public buildings. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments elsewhere in the country, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence.

Social visibility is high. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events and nightlife and a substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist and the Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman; in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.
tangentialFactors:
Local presentation bans exist elsewhere in Mindanao and on nearby islands. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato province prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. No equivalent ordinance is recorded for Caraga, but the pattern is relevant to a visitor routing through northern and central Mindanao.

After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps, evidence that protections collapse in emergency and camp settings rather than only in ordinary policing.

The regional position compares favourably with provinces that have no local ordinance at all, where the absence of a national statute leaves a trans visitor with no discrimination remedy, and unfavourably with jurisdictions offering administrative legal gender recognition, which the Philippines does not.

The national travel-risk scoring gap between LGBTQ+ travellers overall (69) and trans travellers (62) reflects the additional document, presentation and violence exposure that distinguishes trans travel from gay or lesbian travel in the Philippines.

Trans Filipinos may petition a court for a change of gender marker, the only available route after the Clerical Error Law and the Cagandahan ruling removed the administrative path. The pending bill on X and non-binary markers, filed by trans Filipinos, had not been enacted.

The 2023 update to the lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility bars discrimination against clients on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds.

Basic-education settings carry non-discrimination coverage under national rules; outside that context, protection is left to local ordinances. Registered LGBTQ couples in Quezon City can hold a Right to Care Card for medical decision-making, initially in government-owned hospitals.
blindOutOfScope:
No enforcement record for the regional capital's ordinance of 2016 or the provincial ordinances in the two state/provinces within the region is sourced: whether complaints have been filed, how police in the region apply them, and what penalties have resulted remain unresolved.

Whether the diversity and inclusion programme created in 2019 and amended in 2023 has any office, staff or complaint channel operating in the region is not sourced; the reports state only that neither instrument had been implemented as of 2025.

The source material records no region-level data on jail population by gender identity, so it is unresolved whether the segregation practice documented in one other city is applied in the region's own detention facilities.

One source entry for this jurisdiction records no usable finding on LGBT rights, so the regional picture rests on the national framework and on the record of individual local ordinances rather than on a regional survey.
